finding.headline: Retiring at 64 leaves one year before Medicare at 65, so plan for that gap.
details: Medicare generally starts when you turn 65. Your Initial Enrollment Period lasts 7 months, from 3 months before you turn 65 to 3 months after.
If you miss that 7-month window, you may have to wait to sign up and pay a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B coverage. The penalty grows the longer you wait.
For 2027, the 401(k) limit is $25,500, and the IRA limit stays at $7,500. These limits matter for saving before retirement.

finding.headline: About 18 cents of every dollar you earn goes to tax now; in retirement it is about 4 cents.
details: Right now you pay about $16,974 a year in federal, state and payroll tax, out of $94,500 in pay.
In retirement, your withdrawals face a tax rate of about 4%, or about $1,385 a year.
Draw on taxable savings and cash first, then your 401(k), and your Roth last. This is a rough guide, not tax advice.

finding.headline: This household has no children, college, or pet costs to plan for.
details: Family costs are $0 a year, and there are no college or big costs to plan for.
Once retired, the basic costs are about $50,700 a year, or $4,225 a month. Housing is $18,540, food $7,515, transport $12,138, and health $12,475.
Before Medicare at age 65, health premiums are about $10,000 a year. Long-term nursing home care, if needed, runs about $129,575 a year for 3 years.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Your spending now is about $2,674 a year more than your take-home pay, so until you retire the plan takes that from your savings each year. If that is wrong, change your spending now or your pay.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $22,800 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 69 for each of you, which pays about $26,400 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $13,500 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 100. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
